newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bangkok transit scheme may miss deadline - Hopewell.
newsitem.headline: Bangkok transit scheme may miss deadline - Hopewell.

text.p: Thai government delays threaten the timely completion of Hopewell Holding's $3.2 billion Bangkok mass transit project, company Chairman Gordon Wu said on Tuesday.

Hopewell's combined elevated road and rail project, one of three mass transit systems due to be completed in the congested Thai capital within the next five years, has faced continual delays since an initial agreement was signed in 1991.
Wu has consistently blamed the Thai government for the hold-ups.
Hopewell is facing fines over existing delays to the project, which is about 20 percent complete, Wu told reporters after addressing a conference in Bangkok.
"Unless they act quickly we will not see this process ready for the (1998) Asian Games. The ball is definitely in the Thai government's court," Wu said.
The Thai cabinet must approve nine key proposals soon or parts of the project will not be completed on schedule.
Hopewell was required to finish at least two thirds of the system by December 1998, in time to help relieve traffic congestion for the Asian Games to be held north of the capital.
The 44-km (27-mile) project includes a freeway, an elevated train system and the upgrading and elevating of part of the existing state railway system in Bangkok.
Wu said cabinet agreement on the proposed fare structure, land expropriation and technical designs were urgently needed for the project to be completed on time.
Hopewell has suggested train fares for the first year be set at a minimum 10 baht ($0.40) with a 40-km journey costing around 35 baht, Wu said.
For the following six years the firm planned to charge a 15 baht minimum fare, with a 40-km journey rising to 50 baht, he said.
The project financing, including a $100 million loan from Thai financial institutions, was ready to be drawn down as soon as the Thai government agreed to terms, Wu said.

"The Thai banks' commitment to this is very good. But we want to know the enthusiasm of the Thai government. As soon as the ball is back in (our) court we will deliver, we have always delivered," Wu said.
"I don't want to disappoint the Thai people so I would ask the Thai government to hurry up and let's get on with it," Wu said.
